Naturalistic human ECoG · closed-loop translation · research summary

Reading behavior off the cortical manifold

Prior work asked can we decode movement from the brain? and answered in the affirmative. This study poses a different question: what is the geometry of the low-dimensional manifold on which naturalistic behavior is written in human cortex — is it shared across individuals, and can a coordinate on it serve as a clinical biomarker?

Dataset: AJILE12 · human ECoG + pose N = 4 subjects local (1 primary + 3 downloaded) Translational target: psychiatric closed-loop DBS Analysis ~Jul 11 · focused-direction update Jul 16 (below ↓)

Summary

Movement can be decoded from the cortical surface, and coarse behavioral states such as sleep versus conversation are similarly readable; however, decoders are typically built per patient and biomarkers are identified manually, which is limiting for psychiatric implants that must track slow states from sparse labels. This work addresses four questions. Timing: movement is most decodable within a brief (~0.2 s) window, cortical activity leads behavior by approximately 0.5 s, and constraining decoding to be causal (real-time) reduces accuracy — an explicit latency cost for an implant. Drift: within a single session the signal is largely stationary, so a frozen decoder suffices and adaptation confers benefit only when drift is deliberately induced, indicating that short-term deployment may not require continual recalibration whereas multi-day deployment will. Learned alignment: a model aligning neural and behavioral signals was expected to outperform hand-crafted spectral (band-power) features, but did not, under either abundant or scarce labels, and continuous kinematics (movement speed) were not decodable; this null result indicates that band-power is already near the performance ceiling for single-session motor decoding. A more informative analysis set accuracy aside and examined representational geometry: cortical activity occupies a ~2–3-dimensional subspace on which a simple, interpretable α/β “arousal” biomarker separates rest from engagement (AUC ≈ 0.99) in every patient with sufficient data, functions as a closed-loop trigger in simulation (96% sensitivity, ~0.5 false-alarms/hour), and, under a multi-class model, separates all six behavioral states. Two hypotheses were not supported, and each null result is informative: the biomarker did not transfer to a new patient as a drop-in decoder, implicating electrode placement and indicating a need for anatomy-aware features or per-patient calibration; and the hypothesis that the cortical state-map has a common geometry across individuals was refuted (0 of 3 patient pairs exceeded a chance baseline), indicating that what transfers across patients is the biomarker’s α/β spectral signature rather than its geometry. The contribution is therefore not that behavior can be decoded — which is established — but a reframing toward an interpretable, low-dimensional arousal biomarker with the properties of a closed-loop control signal, delimited by clear negative results that localize the central difficulty of cross-patient generalization: a basis for subsequent work toward psychiatric deep-brain stimulation.

Prior work

Established findings relevant to the present questions.

AJILE12 data descriptor

Singh, Peterson, Rao & Brunton, Sci. Data 2022 — 12 patients, 55 days, ECoG + pose + behavioral-state labels.

Significance: the substrate. Defines every signal and label this study reads.

HTNet

Peterson, Rao & Brunton 2021 — cross-participant movement decoding via anatomical region-projection; small fine-tuning reaches per-patient performance.

Significance: transfer works with anatomy-aware, fine-tuned models. Leaves open whether spatial identity is required for any signal to transfer, or whether a distributed signal can transfer without it.

Behavioral-state decoding (direct predecessor)

Alasfour & Gilja, Front. Hum. Neurosci. 2024 — per-participant AJILE12 decoders (talk / TV / sleep) find consistent spectro-spatial features across participants.

Significance: establishes consistency but trains and tests within each participant — no decoder is trained on some patients and evaluated on a held-out one. That test is this study's focus.

Arousal signatures are global & generic

Wen et al. 2016; Bourdillon et al. 2020; Fan et al. 2023; Höhn et al. 2024 — broadband ECoG grows more globally correlated in sleep than wake; spectral/connectivity signatures of arousal are distributed across cortex; a generic property (spectral slope) alone classifies arousal state.

Significance: this predicts, rather than is surprised by, a channel-agnostic feature transferring across montages — narrows this study's real contribution to testing whether the known signal transfers zero-shot across patients, not to discovering that arousal is global.

Neural manifolds

Gallego, Miller & Solla 2018 / 2020 — behavior lives on a low-D manifold, stable for 2 yrs as neurons turn over.

Significance: the reframe. The object of interest is geometry, not per-channel accuracy.

CEBRA

Schneider, Lee & Mathis, Nature 2023 — contrastive latent embeddings of neural + behavior data.

Significance: the method borrowed here (M1/M2), extended to a symmetric two-tower — mostly shown in animals.

Multilingual LLM "lingua franca"

Zhao et al. 2024 — language-specific neurons read in/out, but meaning maps to one shared concept space.

Significance: the metaphor for cross-subject alignment — shared manifold beneath idiosyncratic electrodes.

Closed-loop psychiatric DBS (single-patient trigger)

Scangos et al., Nat. Med. 2021 — a personalized amygdalar biomarker, found over days of monitoring in one patient, triggers stimulation; remission.

Significance: the application ceiling this study aims at — but the biomarker there is per-patient, not transferred.

Longitudinal / periodic biomarkers

Alagapan et al., Nature 2023 — a cingulate biomarker (SDC) tracks depression recovery over weeks across patients. Provenza et al., Nat. Med. 2024 — disruption of neural periodicity (not a snapshot) predicts DBS response in OCD.

Significance: biomarkers can be slow, longitudinal, or defined by temporal structure — not just an instantaneous trigger threshold.

Adaptive DBS is mature — in Parkinson's

Little et al. 2013; Bronte-Stewart et al. 2025 — real-time sensing and stimulation adjustment is validated and long-term deployed in Parkinson's disease.

Significance: contrast case for Phase 2. Adaptive closed-loop DBS is established for movement disorders; psychiatric DBS (this study's target) remains individualized and largely open-loop.

Cross-subject manifold alignment

amLDS / MED-VAE / MindEye2 — align latent dynamics across individuals into a common space.

Significance: the tool for the "lingua franca" test — shared geometry appears only after alignment.

"Which decoder wins?"  →  "What is the manifold, is it shared, and is it a biomarker?"

Modern motor neuroscience shows behavior is written in the geometry of a low-dimensional population manifold — a manifold-based decoder remains reliable for years while a channel-based decoder degrades. From this perspective, "band-power beats the embedding by 0.05 AUC" is the wrong metric. The findings below are interpreted as structural properties of that manifold and its clinical potential.

Analytical progression

For each phase: the question posed, the method, the result, and the decision that followed.

1

Temporal resolution supported

At what timescale is movement legible in cortex — and what does real-time cost?

Did

Swept window length, neural→behavior lag, and causal vs. acausal cost on band-power.

Found

Peak at a ~0.2 s window; neural leads behavior by ~0.5 s; causal-only decoding costs up to +0.20 AUC.

→
Decision: the signal is brief and peri-movement, and real-time carries a "latency tax." This constrains the sampling and actuation cadence for an implant; subsequent phases address which representation to decode.
2

Drift & online adaptation partial

Does the decoder need to adapt online, or is a frozen model enough?

Did

Prequential streaming — static vs. online-SGD vs. sliding-refit — plus a rotation positive control.

Found

Within-session signal is ~stationary (static decoder does not decay); adaptation only helps once drift is induced.

→
Decision: the adaptation machinery works, but AJILE12's within-session drift is too weak to headline. Real drift needs cross-day or stim-logged data — deferred, machinery kept. (Context: real-time sensing-and-adjustment closed loops are already mature and long-term deployed in Parkinson's DBS — Little et al. 2013; Bronte-Stewart et al. 2025 — this phase's open question is whether the same holds for psychiatric targets, not whether adaptive DBS works in principle.)
3

Multimodal alignment — M0 vs M1–M3 negative (informative)

Does a learned neural↔behavior alignment beat hand-crafted band-power — and where?

Did

Compared raw band-power (M0), CEBRA-Time/Behavior (M1/M2), and a symmetric two-tower InfoNCE (M3) across targets, label budgets, subjects.

Found — accuracy

Band-power ≥ learned at full supervision; no low-label win (M3 worst); cross-subject LOSO ≈ 0.49, raw CKA ≈ 0.

Found — structure

Shared space is bidirectional (behavior→reach 0.74); kinematics undecodable (speed R²≤0); coarse state decodes strongly (T5 0.87, T6 ≈1.0).

→
Decision: learned alignment does not improve single-session motor decoding — a clear boundary result. The secondary observations (state ≫ events, bidirectional space) indicate a more productive direction: a shift from scoring decoders to characterizing the manifold.
4

Manifold & biomarker biomarker supported; shared-geometry refuted

What is the manifold's geometry, is there a state biomarker, and is the geometry shared across people?

Did

PCA state & movement manifolds; intrinsic dimensionality (participation ratio); LDA state biomarker; cross-subject Procrustes ("lingua franca").

Found — geometry

State manifold is strikingly low-dimensional (participation ratio 2.6 of 425). In a nonlinear UMAP, Sleep/rest forms a cleanly separated island while the active sub-states (Talk/TV/etc.) blend together (silhouette 0.14). Reach stays diffuse even under UMAP (−0.02) — events do not carve regions.

Found — biomarker

A single linear axis (full-space LDA) separates sleep vs. active at AUC 0.995, α/β-led — the classic cortical rest rhythms, and structurally the quantity identified manually by Scangos et al.

Found — lingua franca

Across 3 subject pairs, 0 beat a label-shuffle null (disparities 0.71/0.36/0.21 vs nulls 0.64/0.53/0.27; p=0.70/0.24/0.34). Shared state-geometry is not supported — a firm negative, not just underpowered. The real cross-subject signal is the biomarker's shared α/β rhythm, not its geometry.

Found — closed loop

As a streaming trigger the biomarker flags the sleep state at 96% sensitivity, 98.9% specificity, 0.5-min latency, and 0.5 false-alarms/hour — Scangos-style closed-loop feasibility.

→
Decision: the manifold is low-dimensional and carries a robust, interpretable state biomarker that functions as a closed-loop trigger. The cross-subject shared-geometry hypothesis did not survive a null test (0 of 3 pairs exceeded chance), a clear negative result. Next steps: clinically relevant target states for the trigger, and a larger cohort to re-examine shared geometry.

Biomarker: representation and example

Representation, with a sample window (sub-01).

X        (895, 425)   =  (895 windows, 85 channels, 5 bands)   # log band-power per 10-s window
bands    [theta, alpha, beta, low_gamma, high_gamma]
weights  (425,)        biomarker = one weighted sum of those features  ->  one number per window
proj     (895,)        the biomarker value.  sample: [-1.05, -3.35, -3.66, -0.17, 12.94, -4.41]   # +12.94 = a sleep window
top wts  ch70 alpha -35.2   ch71 alpha +32.8    # a *local alpha gradient* between two adjacent contacts

Note on ground truth. Windows are non-overlapping and 10 seconds long, but the label each window carries is inherited from the multi-minute behavioral epoch it falls inside (AJILE12's coarse, video-scored annotation). There is no independent, second-scale adjudication of behavior; the results above describe decoding of epoch-level state sampled onto 10-second windows, not second-scale state detection with independent ground truth at that resolution.

Completed — adopt alpha+beta-only as the transfer feature set.

Completed — the movement-confound objection is addressed.

Completed — revised the novelty claim throughout the report.

Broader significance

The findings bear on three areas.

Science

A geometry of behavior

Is there a universal, low-dimensional geometry of naturalistic human behavior in cortex — shared across individuals? An open, fundamental question about neural coding which these data can begin to address.

Clinic

Findable biomarkers

Closed-loop psychiatric DBS currently depends on a single, manually identified biomarker per patient. If states live on a shared, alignable manifold, discovery becomes principled and transferable — a different future for treatment-resistant depression and OCD.

Engineering

Decoders that last

Manifold decoders stay stable for years where channel decoders decay — the difference between an implant that functions briefly and one that remains reliable for years. The same class of problem spans BCI limb-control systems (Hochberg et al. 2012; Flesher et al. 2021), which despite standardized hardware still rely on patient-specific calibration.

Proposed next steps

Some are feasible with current data; others require additional data.

  • Immediate
    Make the biomarker transfer between patients. First result: partial (0.72). A channel-agnostic α/β readout trained on two patients reads a third, uncalibrated, at AUC 0.72 — above chance, and the only cross-patient signal that works. Next: add light per-patient calibration and more patients to push toward the within-patient ceiling.
  • Immediate
    Check if the arousal signal follows a daily rhythm. Track the biomarker smoothly across the full 24 hours instead of in chunks. A gentle rise-and-fall over the day (not just one sleep block) would connect this arousal readout to the temporal-organization biomarkers described in Provenza et al. (2024), where disrupted periodicity — not a snapshot value — predicts DBS response in OCD.
  • Immediate
    Explain why the learned model did not help. Feed the two-tower the raw signal instead of the pre-computed band-power. If alignment only helps then, it shows the simple features already captured everything — turning a negative into a clear lesson about when learned models add value.
  • Immediate
    Give the biomarker a physiological story. It’s a local alpha difference between two neighbouring electrodes — pin down what that is (an arousal/idling rhythm), so it is more than a set of weights.
  • Longer-term
    Graded control, not just on/off. The six behavioral states separate too (0.87), so the readout could adjust stimulation by degree rather than a simple trigger — closer to a real device.
  • Longer-term
    More patients, then clinical data. Download more subjects to properly power the transfer tests, and take the whole pipeline to psychiatric recordings where the slow states are the real target and labels are scarce — the principal translational objective.
  • Longer-term
    Scale to the full 12-patient cohort. Attempted; blocked by disk space. AJILE12 totals ~850 GB; only 3 of 12 subjects (~26 GB) fit in the ~54 GB free at the time of this analysis. With the remaining subjects, test whether the binary arousal transfer holds at larger N, whether the spatial ablation (electrode-identity vs. anatomical ROI, currently underpowered at N=3) resolves, and whether the multi-state transfer — at chance with three patients — reveals a reproducible pattern or is confirmed to be genuinely patient-specific.
  • Longer-term
    Apply the deeper cross-subject models from prior work. Where the simple spectral summary plateaus (multi-state, finer transfer), evaluate HTNet-style region-projection, montage-agnostic foundation models, and domain-adaptation / adversarial alignment. Novelty would lie in whether these enable multi-state or improved cross-patient transfer of naturalistic state that the linear feature cannot — or in demonstrating that they do not, which itself bounds the value of added model complexity.

Update · July 16, 2026

Focused direction

The preceding four-phase analysis (through ~July 11) was broad in scope. This update narrows the work to a single testable, clinically relevant claim, supported by a new cross-patient transfer result.

Why this direction

Selected from the four-phase exploration by four criteria: positive evidence, novelty relative to prior work, clinical relevance, and feasibility with the available data.

Thread exploredOutcomeDisposition as a focus
Temporal resolution (timing)Reproduced established window/lag/causal effectsCharacterization; informs implant design, not a new direction on its own.
Online adaptation under driftInconclusive — within-session data are stationaryDeferred; requires cross-day or stimulation-logged data.
Learned multimodal alignment (two-tower, CEBRA)No improvement over band-powerBounded negative result; set aside.
Manifold geometry shared across patientsRefuted (0 of 3 pairs exceeded a null)Geometry is not shared; not a transferable claim.
Interpretable state biomarker (within patient)Effective, but established in prior work [1]Necessary, but not novel in isolation.
Cross-patient transfer of the biomarkerPositive (0.72), novel, feasible on current dataThe focus — the only thread meeting all four criteria.

Only the cross-patient transfer thread satisfies all four criteria at once: it is the sole cross-patient result with positive evidence; it addresses a gap the prior literature left open (feature consistency was shown, but a transferable decoder was never tested); it targets an open problem in closed-loop DBS (patient-agnostic biomarkers); and it is testable with the available data. It is also narrow, addressing the concern that the four-phase scope was too broad.

Central claim

A single interpretable arousal biomarker that transfers across patients.

The work is narrowed to a single question of clinical relevance: is there a cortical readout of arousal that behaves consistently in a new patient, without retraining? Three lines of evidence support this direction; the third is new:

1 · Same signal in every patient

An α/β readout separates rest from engagement at AUC 0.91–0.998 in all three patients — the same spectral signature each time.

2 · It can drive a device

As a closed-loop trigger it fires reliably in all three (sensitivity 90–96%, ≤0.5 false-alarms/hour).

3 · Cross-patient transfer (new)

Trained on two patients and tested on a third with zero calibration, it reads the unseen patient at AUC 0.72 — the only cross-patient result that beats chance.

Raw electrode channels (sensorimotor ROI-projection, movement target, Phase 3)0.49 (chance)

The comparison is informative: raw channels transfer at chance (0.49) and the manifold shape does not transfer at all (0/3 pairs), but a channel-agnostic spectral summary does (0.72, zero-shot, with room to climb toward the ~0.96 within-patient ceiling with light per-patient calibration). What is shared across brains is the feature, not the geometry — a narrow, testable, clinically relevant basis for the next phase.

Bound. Transfer is specific to the coarse arousal axis. A multi-state readout (3–5 classes) does not transfer across patients (leave-one-patient-out macro-AUC 0.44–0.54, at chance), although states separate well within patient (6-way macro-AUC 0.87). What generalizes across brains is rest-versus-engaged arousal, not activity type.

Update, after decomposition (below). A battery of ablations was run to try to falsify this claim. Most survive it — but the single most important ablation shows a classic 1-feature theta/beta vigilance ratio transfers better than the 35-feature model above (0.83 vs. 0.72). The transferable signal is best described as established vigilance-index physiology, shown here to transfer zero-shot across patients, not a novel multi-feature biomarker. See the section below for the full decomposition.

Decomposing the transfer: global vs. local ablations

An attempt to falsify the channel-agnostic / global-arousal account of transfer, per six pre-registered ablations.

A · Granularity curve falls off systematically

Binary (0.72) → 3-class (0.58) → 4-class (0.54) → 6-class (0.53). Transfer degrades monotonically as the target gets finer — consistent with, and predicted by, prior evidence that arousal signatures are globally distributed and do not carry fine-grained activity identity (Wen et al. 2016; Fan et al. 2023).

B · Spatial-information ablation mixed, small N

Naive electrode-identity (0.70) transferred nearly as well as the channel-agnostic summary (0.72); the 17-region anatomical aggregation did worse (0.38, imputation-heavy with only 3 patients). This does not cleanly confirm "spatial information hurts transfer" — see caveats below.

C · Frequency-band ablation narrows the recipe

Beta alone (0.82) and alpha+beta (0.83) transfer better than all five bands together (0.72). Theta, low-, and high-gamma add noise rather than signal to cross-patient transfer — the biomarker should be defined on alpha+beta only.

D · Electrode-subsampling robustness robust

Transfer survives large montage reductions: even 10 randomly chosen channels reach 0.71 (full montage: 0.72), peaking around 20 channels (0.80). The signal does not depend on a specific, large, or complete electrode set.

E · Awake-rest control rules out motion confound

Sleep vs. Inactive (both motionless) still transfers strongly (0.81) — ruling out gross movement as the explanation. Inactive vs. Engaged (both awake) is at chance (0.34): transfer is specific to vigilance, not to movement or to finer engagement level.

F · Simple-baseline control revises the novelty claim

A classic 1-feature theta/beta vigilance ratio transfers better (0.83) than the engineered 35-feature spectral summary (0.72), consistent with Höhn et al. (2024)'s finding that a single generic spectral property alone classifies arousal state. The transferable component of naturalistic ECoG state is explained by established vigilance-index physiology, not a new learned biomarker.

Net read. The global-versus-local account survives four of six ablations (A, D, E, and the broad thrust of C) reasonably well: a coarse, montage-robust, motion-independent vigilance signal transfers across patients, and it degrades with target granularity. Two results push back on the original framing: the spatial ablation (B) does not cleanly show identity-based features failing and ROI-based features succeeding — with only 3 patients and sparse per-region coverage this ablation is underpowered and should be re-run once more subjects are available. More importantly, the simple-baseline control (F) shows the transferable signal is not new: it is classic theta/beta vigilance physiology.

On narrowness. None of A, C, or F should be read as a novel discovery about arousal physiology — prior intracranial work already shows arousal states produce globally distributed, spatially non-specific, physiologically generic (low-frequency) signatures (Wen et al. 2016; Bourdillon et al. 2020; Fan et al. 2023; Höhn et al. 2024). Given that, the genuinely open and narrow question was whether this specific, known signal class transfers zero-shot to a previously unseen AJILE12 patient with no electrode registration and no calibration — and precisely what does and does not survive that transfer. Revised claim: established vigilance-index physiology transfers zero-shot across AJILE12 patients without electrode registration; six ablations decompose which of its properties (granularity, spatial representation, frequency band, montage size, motion-independence) carry that transfer. This is a demonstration and decomposition of a known signal's cross-patient behavior, not a new biomarker and not a claim that arousal encoding is itself novel. A further caveat on the target: sleep-vs-active is a methodologically easy contrast to decode well (per the same literature) — the evidentiary weight here rests on the transfer-and-ablation methodology, not on the raw AUC.

Method note. All leave-one-patient-out scores here restrict both the held-out test patient and the training pool to patients with ≥10 examples of ≥2 classes for that specific target. Earlier in this session, a version of this analysis that pooled a class-incomplete patient (sub-04, no Sleep/rest examples) into every other patient's training set understated the binary transfer AUC by about 0.07 (0.65 vs. 0.72) — not a labeling error, but a reminder that training-pool composition materially affects LOSO estimates and should be reported explicitly.

Validation across split strategies (within-patient, sub-01). Three splits were compared for the within-patient sleep-vs-active ceiling: a random 70/30 window split (AUC 0.998, the reported ceiling); a split that keeps every window of a given behavioral epoch together but still assigns whole epochs to train/test at random (AUC 0.992 — the small drop is within-epoch autocorrelation, not leakage); and a strict chronological split (first 70% of the recording for training, last 30% for testing), which is undefined for sub-01 because sleep occurs only in the first ~1 hour of a ~16-hour span, leaving zero sleep windows in the held-out 30%. Precisely: the epoch-grouped split (0.992) is not the same test as a chronological split, and the chronological split does not resolve to a number at all for this patient — within-patient validation of this target is confounded with time-of-day in single-session data. This is exactly why the cross-patient leave-one-patient-out result, not any within-patient split, is treated as the primary evidence for transfer in this report.

Not run: full 12-subject LOSO. AJILE12 totals ~850 GB across 12 subjects; only 3 (~26 GB) are downloaded locally and only ~54 GB of disk was free (of a 953 GB volume already at 95% use) — not enough headroom for the remaining 9 subjects (~100–150 GB). All ablations above are therefore a 3-patient pilot; whether the granularity curve, the spatial ablation, and the vigilance-vs-learned-biomarker comparison hold at N=12 is the natural next test.

Novelty and prior work

Positioned within cross-individual decoding of naturalistic behavioral state from intracranial signals.

Established

  • Naturalistic state decodes from spectro-spatial band-power, within subject. The same five bands, linear classifier, and AJILE12 data show that the discriminative features are consistent across participants [1], but no decoder trained on some participants was tested on a held-out one; affective state from band-power was likewise shown within subject [2].
  • Arousal signatures are already known to be global and physiologically generic, not local. Broadband ECoG becomes more globally correlated in sleep than wake [3]; spectral/connectivity signatures of arousal are distributed across cortex rather than confined to specific sites [4, 5]; a single generic property (spectral slope) alone classifies arousal state [6]. This body of work predicts that a channel-agnostic, low-frequency feature should transfer across montages — it is not an open question this study discovers, but a premise this study tests under transfer.
  • Cross-patient transfer that succeeds elsewhere relies on deep, learned, anatomy-aware models. HTNet (a CNN with learned anatomical region-projection and fine-tuning) transfers movement decoders [7]; montage-agnostic foundation models [8] and adversarial/contrastive domain-adaptation methods [9] absorb electrode variability with learned encoders, largely for movement or cued tasks. Whether spatial identity is required for any signal to transfer, or whether a sufficiently distributed signal transfers without it, is left open.
  • Patient-agnostic biomarkers remain a stated open problem in closed-loop DBS. A depression biomarker was identified per patient over days of monitoring [10]; longitudinal/periodic biomarkers exist across small cohorts but are still fit per patient or per cohort [11, 12]; biomarkers that generalize zero-shot, with no patient-specific calibration, are not established.

Contribution (narrow, by design). Given [1]–[6] above, the open and testable question was specific: does a channel-agnostic theta/beta summary transfer zero-shot to a previously unseen AJILE12 patient — no electrode registration, no fine-tuning, no calibration — and precisely what does and does not survive that transfer? This study answers both parts. The signal transfers (mean LOSO AUC 0.72–0.83 depending on feature recipe); finer behavioral-identity targets and raw electrode-indexed features do not. Six ablations (granularity, spatial representation, frequency band, montage size, a motion-confound control, and a simple-baseline control) decompose which properties of the signal carry the transfer. The contribution is this zero-shot demonstration and its decomposition — not a new biomarker, and not a claim that arousal is globally encoded (that is established prior work, [3]–[6]).

Scope. Partial, zero-shot transfer of a binary sleep-vs-active target across three patients — a pilot. Finer targets (3–6 classes) do not transfer (chance-level LOSO). HTNet already established that supervised, anatomy-aware, fine-tuned decoders transfer for movement [7]; this study asks a narrower, different question — whether an already-known, physiologically generic arousal signature transfers with zero calibration — and characterizes, rather than assumes, the answer. Sleep-vs-active is also a methodologically easy contrast per [3]–[6]; the evidentiary weight of this study is in the transfer test and ablations, not the raw AUC.

Key terms

Definitions of the methods referenced above.

LDA — Linear Discriminant Analysis

Each 10-second window is a point in a high-dimensional space (one axis per electrode × frequency band). LDA finds the single straight line through that space along which sleep and active are pulled maximally apart while each stays tight. Projecting a window onto that line gives one number — the biomarker value.

vs. PCA: PCA finds the direction of most variance (ignores labels); LDA finds the direction of most class separation.

Biomarker

A measurable neural quantity that reliably tracks a state of interest. Here: a weighted sum of α/β band-power across electrodes (the LDA axis) whose value rises in sleep/rest and falls in active engagement.

What it marks: a cortical arousal / vigilance axis — not a "sleep detector" but a readout of engaged-vs-disengaged state.

Silhouette score

A measure of how compact and separated clusters are, from −1 to +1. ≈0 means clusters overlap (no clean grouping); >0.5 means very distinct islands.

Here: state 0.14 = weak overall (active sub-states blend) though sleep isolates cleanly; reach −0.02 = no clustering at all.

Procrustes disparity

Take the same landmarks in two systems — here, the average location of each behavioral state in each patient's manifold. Procrustes rotates/scales/reflects one to best overlay the other, then reports the leftover mismatch: 0 = identical shape, 1 = unrelated. Note: with only ~4–6 state-points, almost any two layouts can be overlaid, so even random arrangements score ~0.5 — the number must be judged against a shuffle null, not the raw 0–1 scale.

Here: tested on 3 pairs, none beats a shuffled-label null (p=0.70/0.24/0.34) — shared state geometry is refuted on this data.

CKA — Centered Kernel Alignment

A 0–1 score for how similarly two systems represent the same inputs (1 = identical geometry, 0 = unrelated). Used to compare representations across time-windows and across patients.

Here: cross-subject raw-channel CKA ≈ 0 — electrode space is not shared; the sharing only appears after manifold alignment.

LOSO — Leave-One-Subject-Out

Train the decoder on every patient but one, then test on the held-out patient it never saw. A direct test of whether a model generalizes to a new brain.

Here: LOSO ≈ 0.49 (chance) in this 4-subject pilot — raw transfer failed (HTNet needed 11 patients + fine-tuning).

Two-tower (M3)

Two small networks — one reads brain (ECoG), one reads behavior (pose) — trained so matching brain/behavior moments land at the same spot in a shared space.

What it produced: a bidirectional joint space (decode reach from the behavior side, AUC 0.74) — a capability rather than improved accuracy; it did not outperform band-power.

Participation ratio

Effective dimensionality of the manifold: ≈1 means one axis dominates, ≈D means variance is spread over all D dimensions.

Here: 2.6 out of 425 — naturalistic cortical activity collapses onto ~2–3 effective dimensions.
